# When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

A lot of people get stuck right here. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly, and it's hard to tell which part of you is saying it.

My friend Scott said:

> "Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy."

I used to be all personal trainer and teach persistence on this as the remedy. Keeping at it does help, since a little one who learned to expect being dropped won't trust you right away. But I don't think that explains the adult feeling fully. More importantly, I think it could even be like unintentional gaslighting to the little one to ask to connect with them when you don't believe they're even real. Like when my mom pretended to listen to me when I was young, but even less excusable (from the inner child's view) because she was not asking for my time when she did that. So, it's worth meditating first on why it feels fake.

Sometimes kindness feels scary more than fake. One study's title has a word for that: "[compassion-threat](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31301164/)." People in it with anxious or avoidant attachment reacted to compassion imagery like a threat, and a ten-minute exercise in feeling secure helped with the next try. [Another](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25347984/) found a first try at imagery like that "can be frightening for people who have a tendency to be self-critical." So feeling fake could mean you need a bridge, more than a bigger performance of love.

And picturing one ideal parent seems to help some people. There's a whole method built on it, called the Ideal Parent Figure method. In a [small pilot](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5700488/), seventeen adults with complex PTSD from childhood trauma did five weeks of it and were still doing better eight months later. Seventeen people with nobody to compare them to won't prove the whole method, but it's a start.

For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state, like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn't prove they happened. I'd still hang on to what you felt, even once it's gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You've felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn't just pretending.

## The Parent You Inherited

I'd look at the parent "script" you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it's often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like "You can come back to the table when you're done with your embarrassing crying fit." If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn't allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.

If it's a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you're not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it's one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying "Trust me," of course your little one doesn't answer.

But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don't have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.

## Start With Whatever Showed Up

Your little one wants to play, too, which is why I call the deeper therapy pl/ork, play + work. A lot of the best discoveries come when you're both just messing around, kind of like how kids tell you what's really going on from the back seat, when nobody's looking right at them. Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured.

A lot of what adults tend to lose, your little one still has, like the silliness and the irreverence, the rawness, the creativity, all that, and maybe a connection to the Great Mystery from before any path gave it a name. That's the spark of life they bring, and you get to draw on it and give back, so it's more communion than command. For one example of the spark, there's my post [Treasuring the Inner Child's Gift](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/treasuring-the-inner-childs-gift).

You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you've been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. Maybe it's that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.

How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better. I think a fear that keeps turning up to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you. If it sounds like your little one, though, hear it out the first time it shows up. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you're in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it's your little one asking.

I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder.

You can tell that part something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait and listen patiently. If nothing comes, that's fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It's often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that's what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what you actually know (if you're in danger, get safe first).

Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein came at intuition from two camps of research that were supposed to be at odds, and the paper they wrote together is called [Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0016755). They start from intuition being "sometimes marvelous and sometimes flawed." Yours too, probably. So which kind is a given hunch? How sure it feels won't tell you. Their answer, roughly, is to ask whether the situation is predictable at all, and whether you've had a real chance to learn it. A hunch can pick up on a pattern before your head can explain it, so hear it out, and then let your head have a look. Neither one should decide alone, though. Your head can get tired of not knowing and be glad to hand the whole thing over, to a hunch or to somebody who sounds sure.

Anxiety deserves the same kind of listening. A lot of the time it's a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming: that you'll get overwhelmed, maybe, or that people will laugh at you. It can be right! It's probably been wrong before too, and you know some of those times. So when it's safe to find out, I'd hear it out and then go see. Maybe nobody laughs. (Or they do, and you survive it.) If it might be real danger, though, I'd get some distance first, and find out how right it was later. Same with something a doctor should look at.

Some of it I wouldn't test at all, even when it sounds like a prediction. If a part hesitates about being touched or about sex, that's enough to stop. And if it says no to going deeper in this work, or to an altered state, I'd stop there too. It might not be able to tell you why.

### Two Common Protective Patterns

Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: "You're just making this up." It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That's a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it's experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.

The other one shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it (even a yawn can come with an "I'm so done with this" feeling). It might believe there's no grown-up around who could hold what's coming up. I'd want out too. That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a kind of peer counseling, counts yawning as emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. If you treat either one like an enemy, or like proof that something's wrong with you, it'll probably just think "See? I knew it," and stay in charge. I wonder what it would do if it didn't have to.

### Hear the Protective Part First

Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that's been in your way. I'd still keep it the same. If that voice isn't there in you yet, borrow it from someone who's been safe for you. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?" It might say this will just be one more performance, and you'll fool yourself again.

That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo! If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.

A new roommate doesn't win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector, the grown-up you, earns that protective part's trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.

That part doesn't have to move out. It's been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there's a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. If it says no, I'd listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all. If it's been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn't want to get mine up either. I'd tell it something like, "You don't have to hope yet, I'll keep coming back even when I mess up." Sometimes it doesn't say anything back for a while.

### When to Change the Strategy

Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I'd want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I'd look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I'd work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.

Maybe you've been trying to comfort your little one for weeks, and the words are all there, but the loving grown-up behind them isn't, not yet. Some people at that point might try saying sweeter and sweeter things, and then upon that not working, perhaps just "throw the baby out with the bathwater," and decide reparenting is useless. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.

One more thing about telling whether it helped. A few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I'd take that! But I wouldn't decide from it that the problem's over, or even that the exercise did it, especially if you also slept well for once. Write down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.

How many tries is enough? I really don't know, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it's making things worse, or you just can't do it right now, I'd change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that "nope" sounds like a part of you that's trying to protect you, I'd hear it out first. If it still says no, that's your answer. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don't match yet. Maybe you'll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I'd do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I'd like to hear about it!

Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you're skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people's first guess is that they didn't go deep enough. I don't think that's it, though, and I don't think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn't come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I'd try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn't have to happen after every session.

### When the Urge to Escape Arrives

Sometimes the urge to get away from what's coming up gets a lot bigger. All of a sudden you need a drink, or that ex doesn't seem so bad after all. Some people start a whole new business. If that's you, it might mean you got close to something that really hurts, and that can be progress, honestly! I'd thank whatever part of you came up with the escape plan, and slow down. If it's more than you can hold right now, I'd get someone steady with you.

So why not just blast right past that part, with intensive meditation or psychedelics? Both can get you past the guards before there's a grown-up big enough to hold whatever comes through, so I'd hold off until there's enough Nurturer and Protector around. How much is enough depends on the drug. Like MDMA, San Pedro is more protective and nurturing than many other drugs, especially at lower doses, so you don't need as much Nurturer and Protector built up for it, though you still need some. I already had some from my good childhood to draw on. The first time I took San Pedro cactus, at a medium-low dose, it made me super emotional, and I cried a lot. It was very therapeutic, actually. But I still squandered that opportunity: with a better understanding of reparenting, it could have been much more therapeutic.

Ayahuasca was often much more challenging, because at first I was taking huge doses for ego death. The ayahuasca by itself wasn't exactly spiritual bypassing for me, though. It gave me a connection to divinity, and inner-child reparenting does work best with a little of that. But then I squandered the opportunity to bring that love down from the heavens to my inner child, which led me to be more like a preacher than a fully well-rounded individual who could lead by example.

All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what's real, and that's often the point of them. But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols. I'd say one of the most abused psychedelics (aside from ketamine, if you call that a psychedelic) is 5-MeO-DMT. I have a [guide on that](http://bufo.u-dont-exist.com/). People very often believe you need a huge dose of it for a "full release." They go through all kinds of screaming and shaking, nearly killing themselves, with absolutely zero inner-child work being done. It's all spiritual bypassing.

Your own drug history matters too. If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. I'd look at the drug and the dosage, as well as mindset and setting etc. Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn't automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn't balanced by practicality. "The CIA is mind-controlling me!" is paranoia. "The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates" is paranoia too, but it's practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. "...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!" is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, so I'd avoid those. If you can't clearly understand what happened yourself, get someone qualified to help. And if you have an idea of what happened but aren't sure, ask someone who knows you well.

I went psychotic once on ayahuasca made with pure THH (an alkaloid from the ayahuasca vine) and mimosa hostilis bark, which has DMT in it. THH alone isn't hypnotic (trance-like) enough to keep people safe with higher doses of DMT. When you're in a trance, you can't freak out: no matter how scary something is, it's just like, "Oh, this is scary, OK, oh well." That's not a good excuse to take crazy doses tho. I didn't need anyone to explain that to me, because it was obvious afterward, although it was very helpful that my landlord, a Quaker family friend, was super understanding and talked me down gently. Otherwise the cops might have been called, and I could still be in jail, perhaps, since ayahuasca was illegal there at the time, not to mention I had a bunch of mimosa bark in the house that they might have claimed was for distributing. In general, don't call the cops and expect it to go well. That's a real last resort.

Out of hundreds of times I've taken iboga, there was one time just a small amount of male iboga root bark got me a bit hypomanic, to the point where a thought came: "Everyone should listen to me!" Luckily I was trained in Buddhist meditation, so I immediately challenged it with "Why should anyone listen if they have no interest?" I stopped using iboga for a while after that, and I warn people about that potential issue with [male iboga](http://iboga.u-dont-exist.com/) specifically.

Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I'd be careful with other drugs that mess with what's real too, though I don't mean every drug's dangerous for you. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it's family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. I can't tell you exactly what to do about it, and nobody can tell you for sure what's best for you. There are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can't, get help from trusted advisors.

By trusted, I mean someone you know is trustworthy from a long relationship with them, not someone people on Reddit said was super magical and healing. That's called a crapshoot. It might turn out well, it might not. It might seem like it did, and then later you realize you were duped, as happened to me with [Sidney the iboga shaman](http://sidney.u-dont-exist.com/). A new therapist is not as trusted as an old one. As they say, "new friends are silver, but old friends are gold."

Milder reactions afterward count as caution signs too, like getting confused or spaced out (dissociating) again and again. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you're sober. If you can't tell whether you're safe, I'd treat that as risky. Don't suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.

Be careful what you mix, too, and not just prescribed medicines. Even some basic things like cinnamon can be dangerous (and helpful) with ayahuasca, and doctors don't know about a lot of this. I also learned that mixing acacia confusa with mimosa hostilis is very dangerous. I'd never recommend anyone risk it, since it's highly destabilizing and challenging. I have a [list of things to be cautious about with ayahuasca](http://ayasafety.u-dont-exist.com/) in particular.

Gentle meditation or self-hypnosis is a different story. It can really calm your nervous system down. A lot of people find that a mantra they feel some heart connection to, repeated in their head or out loud, especially with a nice melody, can lower the walls enough for the heart to open up. It's not something to lean on all day as a way of coping, but used as therapy it can be super effective. # Before You Try to Go Deep

How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Try looking around the room, pausing before you act, making a choice and following through on it. If you can't do that because you're basically the frightened kid, leave the deeper conversation until later. You may need somebody steady there with you, or to do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to the child.

And if the grown-up you is there, and it's just how deep you're going that's too much, I'd go shallower. Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there's a grown-up around who can say, "Okay, that's enough for today," and try something gentler instead of giving up on them. Even just saying hi to them with your eyes open, before any imagery, counts.

A full break from your little one is a last resort. Sometimes it isn't up to you, though, like when something's actually unsafe. If you do need one, I'd jot down why, and how far you'd gotten before it got to be too much. A couple of lines on your phone is plenty. After a while away, it gets hard to remember. So once that reason has changed and you want to come back, the note tells you where it was still okay. I'd start there, or somewhere a bit gentler.

## Your Body Might Need Some Love First

If you notice tension in your solar plexus or abdomen, or anywhere else that seems to be keeping you from relaxing into that heart chakra love, try some non-forced, slower exhales and a little gentle self-massage. I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a yin-yang symbol, but you can start with some nice circular or spiral massage right on the tense spot.

If that's not enough, there's deeper somatic stuff like [Shaking](https://www.skool.com/shakingmedicine/about?ref=ee69b2178e96491f88530789dc160291), tapping (EFT), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or some other bottom-up approach.

When your nervous system is flooded, your protective parts are busy with the flood, so they're not going to let your little one come out and talk much anyway. Some people go straight into EMDR on their worst memory before they can even stay in the room. Then they get flooded all over again and decide EMDR doesn't work. Here's a map of what to try when:

Whatever you try from that map, I wouldn't go just by how pleasant a session felt to tell whether it was too much. This kind of work can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes hard dreams, or stuff you'd rather never have met. Even staying present the whole time doesn't tell you enough by itself. It's a bit like the gym, where sore and injured can feel pretty similar that evening, and it's the next few days that tell you which one it was.

So how were the next few days? How did you sleep, and could you get through your day okay? Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? (And was it hard but doable, or just too much? A lot of the time you just know.) If you honestly can't tell yet, I wouldn't rush to call it healing or harm. I'd just make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time, so you learn what made the difference. If you're getting worse, though, change several things at once, and get some support.

Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

### Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over

Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming "shenpa," and she says "[hooked](https://www.lionsroar.com/how-we-get-hooked-shenpa-and-how-we-get-unhooked/)" is a more descriptive translation than the usual "attachment." You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you're supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.

When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

Here's where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That's not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn't mean their boundary crossing indicates “They're evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you're in your happy place.

Feelings about yourself work the same way. "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche's pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don't have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there's nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.

The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with "thought-noting" practice, also isn't healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don't want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.

### Also Look Outward

Once you're in your happy place, look at the other person too, and don't go only by the one fight where they crossed your boundary, or, the other way around, by the one "no" or boundary of theirs that made you mad — after all, they're allowed to say no to you. Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they're not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist [Lindsay Gibson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) wrote the book on this: [*Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People*](https://www.newharbinger.com/9781648481512/disentangling-from-emotionally-immature-people/).) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?

If it's the first, it can seem like you haven't explained yourself well enough yet. You probably have, and it makes more sense to count on what they keep showing you they can do than on the right words finally getting through to them. Maybe what they can do is text you something kind the next day and not bring any of it up.

You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

https://substack.com/profile/355021294-u-dont-existcom/note/c-349048098

If [a relationship](https://romance.u-dont-exist.com) keeps making you feel less safe, meditate on why it makes you feel unsafe, and what keeps you in it. Might it be due to a lack of the healed inner child/inner adult relationship? (If so, you're reading the right guide!) But if they've actually hurt or threatened you, even once, old stuff or not, get safe first, which is not a small thing at all, I know.

If you really did hurt them, repair it. Also easier said than done, but...

You can mean the apology for a start. Then notice what happens next. Are you sorry for what you did, or are you starting to take back the complaint too because they're still upset? Maybe your first explanation sucked. Try again. 😅 And if it fails again, and you've said what you mean, well, you can't guarantee they'll understand it. Guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn't tell you the whole conflict was your fault, nor does it prove they're manipulating you.

Then there are people you're just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--"First impressions are everything," as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you're lovable. Nobody's a reassurance machine. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move. I'm giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present.

If being alone was a big part of what hurt in the first place, then reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Do you have to get yourself sorted out first, so you'll be better company? I really don't think so. If the hurt was being alone, waiting just means more of being alone. So I'd call somebody or show up somewhere, mess and all.

And reaching out doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn't prove you're meant for each other, or that they've earned your trust yet.

I can't tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I'd bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you've already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if one really fits you. Not every one of them has to click (nobody's taking attendance). And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that's where I'd want the Protector paying attention.

### Write It. Don't Send It Yet.

If you've got something burning you up that you wanna say, write it out as a reply. There. That got it out. Ahh. Breathing easier. 😌 But don't send it. Take that breather you earned and then come back to it from a cooler place.

It doesn't mean you need to hide your upset, or apply for a permit to protest, but choose your battles and execute them wisely, so you don't end up regretting how you communicated later. As Lao Tsu might have said (if I could ever have read that whole boring Art of War book), a war with no casualties is the best possible war. When high IQ & EQ communication hits a writer's block, sometimes the best thing is to simply say, "I need some time to think about my response." And if the conflict really requires a response right now, then obviously just do your best rather than wait for the perfect timing.

And yeah, going back to the writer, which is often my inner child when emotions pop up, is part of the process. It's like I'm holding his hand and showing him a better way, not like I just stole his pencil because he wrote something embarrassing. So what was he actually trying to say? A lot of the time it's just "that hurt."

Other times it's "I did this too." My friend Tyler saw a guy smoking in front of a baby and asked him if he thought that was wise. The guy asked if he thought it was wise to mind his own business, and Tyler said, "Well, I believe in Christ, so I thought you might care about life too." Afterward he wasn't sure he'd handled it right, or whether he should have thrown the first stone at all, since he'd smoked in front of a baby himself.

But Jesus also said to take the log out of your own eye first, and then "[you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%207%3A3-5&version=ESV)." That's exactly what made Tyler the right person to say something. If you actually have the problem they have, and you want to call them out for it, call yourself out for it instead. What we came up with was something like, "Hey man, when I was younger I smoked in front of an infant, not realizing how selfish that was, and I notice you doing the same thing. I'd ask you to please have some compassion for him. I have a young child now, so this really touches me."

It's also how your voice sounds, though. You can say all the right words, but if the tone is accusatory, it doesn't matter. Tyler's an evangelical Christian who preaches on YouTube, so it meant a lot to me that he liked this take on what Jesus was saying.

### When Healing Turns Into Checking

You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be completely real while you're checking it for the hundredth time to see whether you've finally grieved it correctly.

Going back can still matter, since realizations are a real part of life. But returning to the same wound can also become a search for certainty in an inherently uncertain existence. Spending all day asking, "Did I process it properly? Did I grieve it enough?" is clearly not what we're after here.

And the checking doesn't always stay in your head. A body scan can turn into one, or a confession, a date, a hookup, one more late-night search, if what you're really after is proof. That you're lovable, say, or that you're not a bad person. It might calm things down for a while, and then the next little wobble matters even more.

If you're feeling guilty because you didn't put your seat belt on, just put it on. If you still want to investigate it later, fine. Perhaps now and then you feel bad about that time you refused to put it on, broke your collar bone in a crash, and then got blamed for not wearing it. That's natural, but doesn't mean there's something new to look at. Then the background checker goes, “But are you really listening?” There it is. Seat belt's on. 😇 Where were we?

Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It's like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don't need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live, stop there.

## You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue

If you don't hear a little kid talking in your head, don't invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you're supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that's what happens for some people, but you might not be some people (hehe).

You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land.  And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it. Maybe what's actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you're in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself.

And it might not be the same order all the time. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first. That's ok, too.

## When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

I've been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though. For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start. They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they've got.

When I talk with folks like that, I mostly want to know what the identity gets them and what it costs, and especially what it's really serving. Some of them even call themselves sovereign, and then somehow there's an urge they have to obey, which sounds more like slavery to me.

This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who's horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they'd rather not have sometimes, and they don't make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you're calm and actually ready. A real parent doesn't get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to be a perfect one.

And if somebody actually wonders whether they're malicious, they'd do better to meditate on it and find out why they're asking before they bring their inner child anywhere near it. Are they really feeling malicious, or is it some voice in their head saying so, like the inherited critic? If some of it turns out to be malice they actually want to act on, the inner child can wait.

In one of the Buddha's own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it's hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it's not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you're the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you'd be the one burning. So it's worth noticing what it's doing to you. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward? Of course not.

The Buddha also told his son that loving-kindness is what gets rid of ill will, and compassion does the same for cruelty. I'm biased on loving-kindness, since it got me out of my depression. For these folks it starts with the grown-up they are now, though, and their little one stays out of it.

As for when their little one gets a turn, I'd say once they've had some bad days where scaring somebody would've felt good, and they didn't do it. Until then it helps a lot to have a real person in their life who likes them and won't laugh along, since loving-kindness is easier to pick up from someone who already has some.

# Appendix

## How This Relates to Schema Therapy

Of the clinical approaches I know, schema therapy is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call [limited reparenting](https://schematherapysociety.org/Limited-Reparenting): within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own "Healthy Adult," who looks after your "Vulnerable Child" and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. Sound familiar? That's a Nurturer and a Protector by other names, and since the therapist's version becomes yours bit by bit, it's borrowed adulthood too.

Where it differs is mostly emphasis, and that depends a lot on who you're seeing. They've got a whole cast of modes. I'd rather keep it to one grown-up with three jobs, and borrowing just one of them is a perfectly good start. Getting yourself out of a bad situation counts as reparenting from day one, too, even if all you did was lock the door. And I wouldn't read your childhood off a picture that pops up, or a knot in your stomach. I'd love to hear what a schema therapist makes of that.

## How This Relates to IFS

Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books [No Bad Parts](https://ifs-institute.com/store/419). Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so "meet the protector first" would fit right in over there. That's a lot of the overlap with this method, right there in the title.

My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. The IFS Institute's [outline of the model](https://ifs-institute.com/resources/articles/internal-family-systems-model-outline) says "everyone has a Self," and that the Self "can and should lead," once your parts stop "blending" with it. I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru. That's still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.

Can't find a calm, compassionate Self in there? Then borrow. One grown-up job at a time, from a friend who'll play Protector for a night, or from something you do, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes (The Parent You Inherited again), until it's yours.

Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I'd call that claim [spiritual bypassing](https://goenka.u-dont-exist.com/). I've had the Higher Self perspective myself, though. It's a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego's illusions, which matches what people say about it. Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part. I don't think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom. It's a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can leave you with less of both. You can see both in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self, often in the same person. [Anthony de Mello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_de_Mello_(Jesuit_priest)) is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego's traps and coming back to the present, and he was a psychotherapist too. He seemed to drift between the two in a way that contradicted itself.

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can't act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn't do much with the Guide at all, which is the opposite problem from IFS, so I'm trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn't exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that's one more problem I'm trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.

IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. Then there's "unburdening," often done after you've witnessed a part's origin story. It can be powerful, sure. It can also get dramatic, all memories and plenty of room for suggestion, which can knock you off balance, especially if you tend to dissociate (DID-like fragmentation included) or to spiritually bypass.

And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it's a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. A gentle practitioner can walk you through it fine. With others, people seem to end up more fragmented than when they started, and an institute with certifications behind the model doesn't by itself make it any truer, or safer for that matter.

So which kind of therapist? I'd learn a bit about the good and bad of both IFS and reparenting first. A grounded, trauma-informed IFS therapist who doesn't put ideas in your head can really help, especially one who gets dissociation. If it's your little one's pain you're dealing with, though, or shame, a good reparenting therapist may be the better fit. Same for attachment wounds. And if you keep abandoning yourself, or there's no inner adult you can count on yet, that's a reparenting therapist's thing too.

### Related Clinical Work

This framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy. I borrow particular distinctions and practices rather than presenting the whole synthesis as their consensus or claiming that their research validates it as a package.

## Teachers and Practice Resources

Daja works with inner-child pl/ork intuitively, through the divine Nurturer and Protector archetypes. Her work is less neuroscience and CBT and more direct archetypal practice, and the three grown-up jobs draw a lot from it. She has a [book](https://a.co/d/7Sa4kP2) and a [free one-hour YouTube training](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL_kbcFWhZK0wJeFUShGvHFZa1u3x7p8Y-&si=Fr0g76mDh8-WLMjM), and she's on [Instagram](http://instagram.com/ihopeyoufindserenity).

Lisa Romano brings more neuroscience and CBT, and her [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2tbMRZKdHJ4) is a good place to start. She makes the point that remembering the specific details of childhood trauma isn't necessary, because the felt body knows what needs to come up. [Key](https://open.substack.com/users/432335983-key-to-enlightenment?utm_source=mentions) developed the Guide's sense of direction, and the identity and differentiation work from Bowen I mentioned earlier. She led a [guided inner-child meditation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UkVlDixqqA0) in Nairobi in January 2026 for twenty people, and it's up on YouTube.

I don't know of a resource to find a perfect inner child therapist, and there are none which work with my guide yet, (although I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them). The best I could suggest at the moment is to search [Open Path Collective](https://openpathcollective.org/pricing-and-eligibility-for-affordable-therapy/) (or a similar resource in your country), which lists thousands of affordable therapists. Filter for  Schema Therapy, since that's the one with the most similarity to my guide, but you'll find about 10x more Internal Family Systems therapists, which also overlap with reparenting in many ways. You can often find [even more Schema therapists at the official site](https://schematherapysociety.org/Search?&tab=1): 3x more on that page for NYC than via Open Path search when I checked. And for bottom-up support, there's my [Somatic Therapies Guide](http://somatic.u-dont-exist.com/), the same map as in Your Body Might Need Some Love First.
